items.title: 40 anni dalle Assisi Declarations, rilanciata l’eredità con “Fare pace con la natura”
items.description: Dal messaggio di Assisi, nasce “Fare Pace con la Natura”, l’incontro promosso dal WWF Italia il 28 ottobre 2026, dalle 10.30 alle 12.00, al MAXXI di R
items.body: In evidenza WWF Italia: 60 anni per la natura In evidenza Il Panda Siamo Noi In evidenza L'orso bruno marsicano In evidenza Adotta una specie 40 anni fa, il 29 settembre 1986, ad Assisi il WWF riunì le principali religioni del mondo intorno a un’idea allora rivoluzionaria: prendersi cura della natura è una responsabilità comune dell’umanità. In occasione del 25° anniversario del WWF International, il Principe Filippo, Duca di Edimburgo e allora Presidente del WWF International, promosse l’incontro che portò alle Assisi Declarations, con cui le diverse tradizioni religiose riconobbero nella tutela della natura non soltanto una questione ambientale, ma una responsabilità morale e spirituale condivisa. Poche settimane dopo, il 27 ottobre, Giovanni Paolo II convocò ad Assisi la Giornata mondiale di preghiera per la pace, dando origine a quello che sarebbe diventato lo “Spirito di Assisi”: il dialogo come strumento per superare le divisioni e costruire pace. 40 anni dopo, natura e pace sono ancora più profondamente intrecciate. Secondo il Programma delle Nazioni Unite per l’Ambiente (UNEP), il 2025 ha registrato il più alto numero di conflitti armati dalla Seconda guerra mondiale. Guerre che, oltre al loro drammatico costo umano, lasciano dietro di sé ecosistemi distrutti, acqua e suoli contaminati, perdita di terre agricole e una crescente pressione sulle risorse naturali. Non può esserci una pace duratura in un pianeta degradato. “Fare Pace con la Natura” Da questa convinzione nasce “Fare Pace con la Natura”, l’incontro promosso dal WWF Italia il 28 ottobre 2026, dalle 10.30 alle 12.00, al MAXXI di Roma, nell’ambito delle celebrazioni per i 60 anni del WWF Italia. A confrontarsi saranno don Paolo Cristiano della Comunità di Sant’Egidio, Stefania Divertito, giornalista e scrittrice, Antonello Pasini, fisico del clima del CNR, Antonio Spadaro, Sottosegretario del Dicastero per la Cultura e l’Educazione della Santa Sede, e Michele Valensise, Presidente dell’Istituto Affari Internazionali. Modera Alessandra Prampolini, Direttrice Generale del WWF Italia. L’incontro sarà aperto da Dante Caserta, Direttore Affari Legali e Istituzionali del WWF Italia, e concluso da Luciano Di Tizio, Presidente del WWF Italia. “40 anni fa ad Assisi il WWF contribuì ad affermare che prendersi cura della natura è una responsabilità comune. Oggi quel messaggio è ancora più urgente. Le guerre hanno innanzitutto un costo umano drammatico: uccidono, costringono milioni di persone a lasciare le proprie case e distruggono comunità. Ma devastano anche ecosistemi e risorse naturali, lasciando ferite che durano per generazioni. Allo stesso tempo, crisi climatica, perdita di biodiversità e scarsità di risorse possono acuire disuguaglianze e generare conflitti. Il Pianeta e le future generazioni non possono subire la follia della guerra tra gli uomini e di questi contro la natura. Fare pace con la natura significa riconoscere la stretta interdipendenza tra la Casa comune e i suoi abitanti e costruire le condizioni per un futuro più sicuro e pacifico”, dichiara Dante Caserta, Direttore Affari Legali e Istituzionali del WWF Italia.  60 anni per la Natura In azione da sessant’anni per la Natura. Ed è solo l’inizio Nel sessantesimo anniversario celebriamo ciò che abbiamo costruito e riaffermiamo ciò che continuiamo a fare: proteggere, rigenerare, educare, ispirare. Da sempre proteggiamo habitat, specie e paesaggi, costruendo… Scopri di più

items.title: La salute di città e cittadini si misura dal ronzio delle api
items.description:
Il nuovo report “La città degli impollinatori” per la decima edizione di Urban Nature: il 3 e 4 ottobre appuntamento nelle piazze italiane 
The post L
items.body: In evidenza WWF Italia: 60 anni per la natura In evidenza Il Panda Siamo Noi In evidenza L'orso bruno marsicano In evidenza Adotta una specie Il nuovo report in occasione della decima edizione di Urban Nature Gli ambienti urbani che offrono condizioni favorevoli agli impollinatori sono anche ambienti più sani, vivibili e resilienti per le persone. È questo il messaggio al centro del report “La città degli impollinatori: più spazio alla natura, più benessere per le persone”realizzato dal WWF in occasione della decima edizione di Urban Nature 2026: il Festival della natura in città, che si svolgerà in oltre 100 piazze italiane nel weekend del 3 e 4 ottobre. Immagine generata con AI La biodiversità in città Le città ospitano una biodiversità spesso sorprendentemente ricca, costituita da numerose specie vegetali e animali, tra cui gli impollinatori, organismi fondamentali per il funzionamento degli ecosistemi e per la produzione di molti degli alimenti da cui dipendiamo. La presenza di comunità abbondanti e diversificate di impollinatori è generalmente associata ad ambienti urbani ricchi di vegetazione, con una maggiore disponibilità e qualità di habitat, minori livelli di inquinamento e una più elevata capacità di adattarsi agli effetti della crisi climatica. Le stesse caratteristiche che favoriscono gli impollinatori in città – presenza di alberi, prati e fiori, suoli permeabili e una migliore qualità ambientale – contribuiscono anche a migliorare il benessere e la salute delle persone. Alla realizzazione del report ha contribuito anche ISDE –Associazione Medici per l’Ambiente – che parteciperà all’evento del 3 e 4 ottobre di Urban Nature nelle piazze italiane. Oltre i 3/4 delle principali colture alimentari mondiali dipendono dall’impollinazione Oltre il 75% delle principali colture alimentari mondiali dipendono, in misura parziale o totale, dall’impollinazione animale, un servizio ecosistemico essenziale che garantisce la produzione e la qualità di molti degli alimenti che arrivano ogni giorno sulle nostre tavole. Eppure, questi preziosi alleati stanno vivendo un declino senza precedenti: a livello europeo, infatti, quasi il 40% dei sirfidi, il 15% delle farfalle e il 10% delle api selvatiche registrano popolazioni in costante contrazione. Le principali cause del loro declino sono collegabili alla perdita e frammentazione degli habitat, l’intensificazione agricola, l’uso di pesticidi, l’inquinamento e dagli effetti della crisi climatica. Il modello della “Città degli impollinatori” Di fronte a questa emergenza, il WWF propone il modello della “Città degli impollinatori”: una visione che considera gli spazi urbani come parte di una vera e propria rete ecologica. Parchi, prati fioriti, alberature, orti urbani, balconi e tetti verdi sono habitat preziosi sia per gli impollinatori sia per contribuire a rendere le città più fresche, resilienti, meno inquinate e più vivibili per le persone. Il report "La città degli impollinatori" Più spazio alla natura, più benessere alle persone Scopri Il report sottolinea come ogni scelta, pubblica e privata, conti e possa avere un effetto moltiplicatore: la riduzione dell’uso dei pesticidi, la scelta di specie vegetali autoctone e diversificate, la presenza di fioriture distribuite lungo l’anno, il mantenimento di aree naturali e seminaturali e la creazione di piccoli habitat diffusi sono interventi che, se integrati tra loro, possono rafforzare la biodiversità urbana e migliorare la qualità degli ambienti per i cittadini. Gli spazi natura WWF Di fronte alle opportunità che si presentano per migliorare la qualità di vita e il  benessere delle persone con la tutela e l’incremento della natura in città, il WWF risponde da anni con gli Spazi Natura WWF, un fondo che si pone un unico obiettivo, quello di riportare la natura al centro della vita delle persone, creando nuove gemme di biodiversità nei luoghi in cui oggi sono più necessarie: scuole, strutture sanitarie, spazi pubblici e privati, strutture ricettive, aziende, istituti penitenziari e altri contesti urbani ad alta fragilità ambientale e sociale. Grazie ad iniziative come le Oasi urbane, le Aule Natura, le Oasi in Ospedale il WWF si impegna a far tornare il verde nelle nostre vite, rafforzando la biodiversità urbana a favore delle persone, in particolare delle categorie più fragili. Per Urban Nature 2026, “il miele si fa cura” Presso gli stand di Urban Nature i volontari distribuiranno i vasetti di miele “Il miele si fa cura” prodotto da apicoltori impegnati nella conservazione della biodiversità e nella protezione degli impollinatori selvatici. Il messaggio di Urban Nature si inserisce anche nel percorso di attuazione della Nature Restoration Law che, all’articolo 8, stabilisce obiettivi specifici per il ripristino degli ecosistemi urbani, riconoscendo il ruolo del verde e della natura in città anche nelle strategie di adattamento alla crisi climatica. Aumentare e migliorare il verde urbano, la copertura arborea e gli habitat naturali può contribuire a ridurre l’effetto “isola di calore”, migliorare la qualità dell’aria, ridurre il consumo e l’impermeabilizzazione di suolo, tutelare gli impollinatori e rendere le città più sicure, sane e resilienti secondo l’approccio One Health, che riconosce l’interdipendenza tra salute umana, animale e degli ecosistemi. Il Regolamento stabilisce una tabella di marcia chiara – nessuna perdita netta di verde urbano e di copertura arborea entro il 2030 rispetto ai livelli del 2024, e un incremento progressivo a partire dal 2031 – e il WWF chiede a Ministero dell’Ambiente, Regioni e Comuni di attuarla senza ritardi, mettendo a disposizione degli enti locali dati aggiornati e risorse adeguate. Con Urban Nature, il WWF sarà presente in oltre 100 città italiane con stand informativi dove sarà possibile incontrare volontarie e volontari del WWF e scoprire il valore degli Spazi Natura WWF. Sarà inoltre possibile partecipare alle iniziative locali, organizzate dalla rete di volontari WWF e dalle Associazioni Amiche di Urban Nature: ANMS, ISDE, ISPRA, AIIG, APID, ACP, AIGAE, Orti Botanici e altre associazioni locali. Tra gli appuntamenti in programma, anche gli aperitivi scientifici organizzati da WWF Young nella serata di venerdì 2 ottobre.Ragazzi e famiglie potranno inoltre scoprire il valore della Natura in città prendendo parte ad attività outdoor, laboratori didattici, passeggiate naturalistiche, eventi nei musei scientifici e tante altre iniziative. L’evento è patrocinato dal Ministero dell’Ambiente e della Sicurezza Energetica, ISPRA e da ANMS.   Urban nature 2026 Sabato 3 e Domenica 4 ottobre saremo presenti in più di 100 piazze italiane con i nostri stand  per raccontare il valore della Natura in città ai cittadini, attraverso la distribuzione del miele WWF, che aiuterà a creare il Fondo Spazi Natura WWF.  Vivi la tua città… Scopri di più

items.description:
I risultati dell'indagine promossa da WWF e Movimento Laudato Si' mostrano che per i cittadini le risposte delle istituzioni sono insufficienti
The po
items.body: In evidenza WWF Italia: 60 anni per la natura In evidenza Il Panda Siamo Noi In evidenza L'orso bruno marsicano In evidenza Adotta una specie Negli ultimi cinque anni nove italiani intervistati su dieci hanno vissuto eventi climatici estremi come ondate di calore, piogge intense e siccità. È quanto emerge dall’indagine* partecipata “La crisi climatica è già qui: cosa sta cambiando per te?”, promossa da WWF Italia e Movimento Laudato Si’ insieme ad altre realtà civiche, con Green&Blue di Repubblica come media partner. Il questionario, distribuito a partire dal 5 giugno fino al 15 settembre, è stato sviluppato con il supporto scientifico della divisione REMHI (Modelli Regionali ed impatti geo-idrologici) del CMCC – Centro Euro-Mediterraneo sui Cambiamenti Climatici, che ne ha garantito il rigore terminologico e la coerenza con la letteratura scientifica e normativa. L’indagine ha raccolto le risposte di 2.423 cittadini e cittadine maggiorenni residenti in tutte le regioni italiane*. Gli eventi estremi ormai parte della quotidianità La prima indicazione significativa è quanto gli eventi estremi facciano ormai parte della nostra vita, modificando la quotidianità e le abitudini di ciascuno di noi. L’89% di chi ha risposto dichiara, infatti, di aver vissuto almeno un evento estremo nella propria zona negli ultimi cinque anni. A dominare sono le ondate di calore, indicate come frequenti**dal 97%, seguite da precipitazioni intense (83%) e siccità (74%). E gli effetti si sentono nella vita di ogni giorno: il 96% ha sofferto il caldo negli spostamenti quotidiani, il 91% ha faticato a lavorare o studiare e il 63% ha avuto problemi respiratori o affaticamento. Più di una persona su due ha vissuto problemi di fornitura energetica o blackout. La percezione del rischio è altissima: il 95% ritiene che gli eventi estremi siano aumentati nella propria zona e il 93% considera necessario rafforzare prevenzione e adattamento. Eppure, le risposte concrete risultano spesso essere limitate e per lo più al livello individuale o famigliare. Molte persone hanno cambiato le proprie abitudini, pianificando diversamente la giornata per evitare il caldo (92%) o proteggendo la casa (88%), ma gli interventi che richiedono più impegno sono meno diffusi: solo la metà dei rispondenti dichiara di aver installato o migliorato condizionatori o ventilazione, una quota ancora minore invece schermature solari (28%), nuove piantumazioni (14%). E solo l’11% ha partecipato a reti di aiuto nel quartiere o nella comunità. Il peso sui bilanci familiari Il clima pesa anche sui bilanci familiari. L’85% segnala un aumento delle spese per il raffrescamento, e una persona su tre dichiara di aver subìto danni materiali o economici. Tra queste, la fascia più frequente è quella tra 1.000 e 5.000 euro. A questo si aggiunge una tutela assicurativa fragile: più di un terzo dei rispondenti dichiara di non avere alcuna copertura contro i danni da eventi estremi e, tra chi ha chiesto un rimborso, meno della metà lo ha ottenuto per intero, mentre il 48% solo in parte. Due persone su tre hanno atteso da uno a sei mesi. Non sorprende che una persona su due dichiari di non essere del tutto certa di avere le risorse per investire in prevenzione. Mentre le persone cercano di adattarsi al clima che cambia, l’azione delle amministrazioni sembra essere poco percepita, soprattutto sul fronte strutturale. Le misure più notate sono le disinfestazioni contro zanzare e altri parassiti e le allerte via SMS, telefono o media, cioè interventi di comunicazione e di emergenza. Molto meno percepiti sono i piani di emergenza locali, il ripristino della natura per prevenire le alluvioni e le opere per rendere accessibili le emergenze a chi ha disabilità. Nel confronto, va tenuto conto che chi risponde tende a valutare più favorevolmente le proprie azioni di quelle delle istituzioni, forse anche perché non sempre le azioni delle amministrazioni locali sono conosciute e certamente non sono ancora inserite in un contesto nazionale, visti i ritardi nell’attuazione del Piano Nazionale di Adattamento ai Cambiamenti Climatici. Il ruolo di Urban Nature La lotta alla crisi climatica non può prescindere dal ruolo della natura nelle aree urbane. Dove presente il verde mitiga le ondate di calore e le alluvioni. Per questo, Il 3 e 4 ottobre torna Urban Nature, l’iniziativa nazionale del WWF, giunta alla sua decima edizione, che coinvolge i cittadini nella tutela della natura in città, per difendere la biodiversità urbana e promuovere ambienti più sani e sicuri. L’evento di quest’anno sarà diffuso in oltre 100 piazze italiane, con stand e iniziative per valorizzare la natura urbana, in linea con l’impegno del WWF per rigenerare gli spazi verdi cittadini. Il sondaggio di YouGov Occorre sottolineare che i risultati del sondaggio condotto da YouGov alla fine di agosto 2026[1] su sei Paesi europei -Regno Unito (Gran Bretagna), Italia, Francia, Germania, Spagna e Danimarca, offrono il contesto dell’indagine condotta dal WWF in Italia. In particolare, Francia, Italia e Spagna sono i Paesi nei quali si è più consapevoli del legame tra ondate di calore e cambiamento climatico. In tutti i Paesi c’è un’altissima insofferenza verso chi tende a sottostimare l’anomalia rispetto al passato e la portata delle ondate di calore. Da rilevare che in Italia un’alta percentuale di cittadini ha sperimentato personalmente gli incendi e tempeste/alluvioni, come mostra la tabella. Altissima la consapevolezza che le azioni per far fronte alla crisi climatica portano benefici alle persone (vedi tabella che segue) e che mitigazione (taglio delle emissioni climalteranti) e adattamento (misure per adeguare economia, infrastrutture e società al cambiamento climatico già in atto, nonché considerare e prevenire i rischi) sono entrambe importanti e vanno condotte insieme. Systematic overview of climate actions for health in cities

Systematic overview of climate actions for health in cities
                        Emma Hutchinson

AbstractMany climate change adaptation and mitigation actions in cities have potential co-impacts for health. This overview of relevant systematic reviews appraises and summarizes available evidence of the effects of implemented city-level actions addressing climate change and health impacts. On the basis of an assessment of confidence in the findings of the 60 reviews identified, the findings from 49 were included in the analysis. Most evidence focused on climate mitigation actions in the transport and buildings sectors and on urban form. Health co-benefits mainly resulted from increased active transport or improved housing. Where reviews provided measures of effect, they suggested only modest impacts on climate and health outcomes from single-sector actions. We found no published evidence of city-wide implementation of cross-sectoral transformative actions needed to achieve climate change targets and large-scale health co-benefits. More ambitious policies, together with rigorous evaluation of their impacts, are needed to attain and demonstrate these outcomes.

                            Climate Change Adaptation Strategies in Urban Planning

MainMultisectoral mitigation and adaptation actions are required to counter the climate crisis1. Global and national actions to address upstream causes (for example, fossil fuel use2) alongside implementation of city policies (for example, transport, urban planning3) are needed to achieve rapid, deep reductions in greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions and thus limit global temperature increases to well below 2 °C (ref. 4).Increasingly, there is recognition that such actions have potential co-benefits for health such as from reduced air pollution, which could increase motivation and public support for achieving deep cuts in emissions3,5,6,7,8,9,10. However, trade-offs between climate action and health outcomes are also possible, necessitating careful design and implementation to achieve optimal effects. Transformative actions, addressing the systemic drivers of GHG emissions, are needed to achieve net zero emissions over coming decades and capitalize on the health (co-) benefits, as well as supporting effective adaptation responses in cities10,11,12.We aimed to synthesize the available evidence through an overview of relevant systematic reviews—a method that transparently collects and appraises all the rigorous findings on a topic13,14,15,16. This umbrella review summarizes the findings from systematic reviews of implemented climate actions with health co-impacts, and vice versa, in cities. By presenting evidence on the climate and health outcomes from these actions across sectors, we aimed to identify both which actions are effective and how they can be effectively implemented, providing evidence for actions that deserve priority attention. This overview constitutes one output of the Pathfinder Initiative, which works with relevant networks (for example, the Carbon Disclosure Project (CDP) and the Carbon 40 Cities (a global network of initially 40 cities working together to address climate action (C40 Cities))) to support urban decision-making14 and improve methods of primary research and evidence synthesis on the health effects of climate change mitigation actions15,16.ObjectivesWe conducted an overview of systematic reviews (umbrella review) published between 2009 and 202417 to synthesize evidence of the effectiveness of implemented city-level actions whose primary or secondary purpose was both to achieve: (1) the mitigation of climate active pollutants (CAPs) (GHGs and black carbon) or adaptation to the impacts of climate change and (2) a health (co-) benefit related to the same action or actions.We included both adaptation and mitigation because some actions address both, and there is potential for synergies and trade-offs between them. Improved governance can help cities shift from undertaking isolated, incremental projects to fostering the multisectoral systemic change necessary for deep decarbonization and large-scale health co-benefits. We therefore also identified critical policy implementation gaps, potential structural barriers and the requirements for effective governance.ResultsSearch results and included reviewsOf the 5,550 records identified from the literature search, screening of titles and abstracts identified 198 reports for full-text assessment, of which 60 reviews were critically appraised, and consequently 49 systematic reviews that provided sufficient confidence in findings for data extraction and synthesis were included (Fig. 1). Most reviews included component studies from high- or middle-income countries (50 reviews), with limited information from low-income settings (10 reviews). The confidence in component studies was mixed and was often assessed as low by review authors (12 reviews) or not reported at all (29 reviews). Our assessment of confidence in the findings of the reviews themselves indicated the majority to be of low confidence (n = 43), and some (n = 11) were of critically low confidence (see ‘Assessments of confidence in findings’). Three meta-analyses18,19,20 and two umbrella reviews21,22, which had different objectives to the current work, and generally did not cover the same studies, were included because they contained relevant evidence21,22. Some studies conducted a review as part of a specific study, such as a health impact assessment23 or other study design24.Fig. 1: PRISMA diagram of included studies.Full size imageaSearch undertaken for the Complex Urban Systems for Sustainability and Health (CUSSH) Project123, but findings not previously published. To ensure a comprehensive retrieval of relevant literature, the database searches were executed independently on three separate occasions. PRISMA 2020 flow diagram for updated systematic reviews adapted from ref. 90, licensed under CC BY 4.0.Assessments of confidence in findingsThere are concerns about the confidence of the findings for most reviews (Fig. 2a; Supplementary Information ‘Risk of bias assessment of included reviews (AMSTAR2)’ includes more details). A lack of specification of the intervention conditions and study designs was frequently observed: the Population, Intervention, Comparison and Outcome (PICOS) statement and study design criteria were reported in 60 percent (n = 37) and 43 percent (n = 26) of the reviews, respectively. In fewer than half of the reviews, independent screening (n = 26, 43%) and data collection (n = 20, 33%) by two or more team members were reported. Even though the searches were classified as being adequate in most cases (n = 48, 80%), most reviews were restricted to peer-reviewed literature (that is, they did not incorporate gray literature), in English, and hardly any tested formally for publication bias (n = 1, <2%). Most reviews reported a direction of effect (for example, 20/49 for environmental outcomes). Very few reviews calculated effect sizes using consistent metrics, nor meta-analyzed the findings to improve statistical power and explore heterogeneity (n = 7; 12%). In summary, out of 60 systematic reviews, only six18,20,25,26,27,28 were rated as having medium or high confidence in our assessments, all from the buildings, transport and urban form sectors (Fig. 2b). Most reviews in all sectors were rated as of low confidence, and there was no evidence of improved confidence in the reviews over time (Fig. 2c). A further 11 reviews (one of which covered two sectors) were rated as of critically low confidence, the results of which are not discussed further or presented in the results (Table 1)23,24,29,30,31,32,33,34,35,36,37.Fig. 2: Results of confidence assessments in included reviews.Full size imagea, Fulfillment of the 16 domains. b, Confidence assessment of the reviews by sector. c, Confidence assessment by year (H, High; M, Moderate; L, Low; CL, Critical low). (Absolute numbers of respective studies within each bar). Confidence assessments were performed using the critical appraisal tool—AMSTAR2—upated to allow assessment of varied study types (ref. 121). QEDs, quasi-experimental designs, also called nonrandomized studies of intervention effects; RCTs, randomized controlled trials; Q, question.Table 1 Summary of implemented actions at city level towards sustainability and healthFull size tableResults by sectorResults of the 49 included systematic reviews are summarized by sector in the following sections and in Table 1 (detailed findings are given in the Supplementary Table 1). The majority described actions relating to transport (n = 25) and to changes in urban form (n = 27), followed by buildings (n = 13). Few reviews were related to the food (n = 3) and waste (n = 3) sectors. One of the transport-related reviews26 was an update of an earlier review25. The sectors covered by the evidence synthesis literature summarized here reflect the types of primary study available38. The types of action identified reflect the relative balance between climate and health actions at national and subnational levels. In particular, where local governments have a greater role in developing and implementing policies and programs—as in the cases of transport, built environment and urban form—it is understandable there would be greater frequencies of studies.In reviews where health impacts were the primary focus, environmental impacts were generally not directly assessed. In reviews assessing environment impacts as a primary focus, health impacts were often not explicitly reported or quantified. However, all reported studies had health relevance, and where explicit health outcomes were not reported, they included environmental exposures that would be highly likely to result in positive health outcomes (for example, from reduced air pollution), as per our framework for population-level impacts on environment and health and our inclusion criteria (Fig. 3; see Table 2 and Table 3). Limited evidence was identified on factors facilitating or impeding implementation (7/49 reviews).Fig. 3: Framework for population-level impacts on environment and health from city-level actions to address climate change, showing linkages for adaptation and mitigation.Full size imageThe gray arrow refers to the link for mitigation action only.Table 2 Pathways affecting healthFull size tableTable 3 Inclusion criteria (PICOS statement), adapted for umbrella reviewsFull size tableTransportClimate mitigation interventions in the transport sector can improve health through two main health co-benefit pathways—improved air quality and increased physical activity (Table 1) in both low- and middle-income country and high-income country settings. However, health co-impacts through improved air quality were reported more often in low- and middle-income countries and physical activity in high-income countries. Health benefits through improved air quality depended on intervention scale and baseline emissions. The most frequently reported actions were traffic-control policies, including traffic restrictions and congestion charging zones and improvements in public transport infrastructure (Table 1), whereas the need for evaluation for a broader range of health and environmental co-benefits beyond the primary policy was often not met39,40.Behavioral changes to preferred modes of transport, away from private vehicle use, towards public transport or more active forms of travel, were influenced by urban form. Factors that appeared to mediate the effects of transport policies and health outcomes (implied41 or estimated40, where reported) included: journey distances, urban density and destination accessibility. Potential increases in road injuries were mitigated through urban design interventions (for example, speed restrictions, traffic lane separation). Car sharing was found to reduce car ownership41 and increase physical activity. Incentivizing giving up workplace parking rights was found to decrease solo driving and CO2 emissions while increasing walking40. Switching to electric vehicles reduced CO2 per vehicle kilometers traveled (VKT) substantially (up to 20%, even when electricity was coal powered), although urban-to-rural displacement of exposure to CO2 was suggested42. Fuel switching from petrol to natural gas failed to reduce particulate matter with a diameter of 10 μm or smaller (PM10) (increasing by 15%) in one study, although other forms of emission reduction (for example, low-emission zones) were associated with decreases in PM10 (up to 17%) (ref. 43). E-scooters were reported to have climate mitigation potential, provided use is complementary to active transport and if lifespan, vehicle charging and equitable/equal access and road safety are considered44.BuildingsWe found limited evidence on actions to reduce energy use45,46,47. Most evidence related to home energy efficiency improvements (for example, insulation for warmth). These measures were associated with appreciable health gains, mainly from improvements in thermal comfort (which are related to improved cardiovascular health48,49) (Table 1) and some improvements in social conditions28. Two reviews also reported impacts on household air pollution, including decreased indoor air quality if ventilation measures were inadequate24,50. Variable results were reported in reducing air pollution from improved fuel for cookstoves and banning coal (with some component studies reporting up to 70% reduction in PM and black smoke)43,51, with consequent benefits to health from banning coal (5–10% decrease in mortality rates)51. Review evidence of implementation of passive cooling measures has increased recently45,46,47,52,53, with reduced energy use reported in some reviews. Moderate to substantially lower carbon footprints from sustainable design and construction (median value 52% less than the comparator) were reported, although not at the city level54. Most evidence on green roofs/walls reported environmental benefits (for example, reduced urban heat exposure and energy use and some reductions in air pollution) with implications for health25,26,34,46,53.WasteEffective mitigation approaches included the use of biodigesters with biogas collection and reuse as energy. Evidence on environmental impacts from recovering energy from solid waste was mixed. An estimated decrease in carbon dioxide equivalent (CO2e) per ton of organic waste from anaerobic digestion and aerobic composting was documented55 (Table 1).Substantial harms to human health were associated with exposure to solid waste incineration including adverse female, maternal and child health outcomes such as increased mortality and cardiovascular disease among women, pre-term births and congenital anomalies56.FoodNo reviews of implemented actions for sustainable diets in urban areas were identified, although they exist at the national level57 (Table 1). All identified reviews in the food sector at city level related to urban agriculture32,58,59 (Table 1). Increasing production and consumption of locally sourced foods (for example, through urban agriculture) can reduce emissions and energy use and enhance biodiversity but were considered unlikely to improve health unless accompanied by dietary changes, such as towards locally produced fruits and vegetables58,59. Climate adaptation through urban agriculture was considered in two reviews (Table 1)58,59.Evidence from low-income settings suggested that locally grown food could increase household food availability and improve incomes45. Evidence on reducing food waste was lacking.Urban formMost of the evidence on improving liveability focused on increasing walkability to reduce motor vehicle use, through urban planning (for example, provision of walking and cycling paths; ten reviews), street redesign (six reviews), improving access to recreational facilities (four reviews) and increasing residential density and changes to land use (six reviews) (Table 1). Most reviews reported that measures were associated with increased physical activity (n = 14) and some with a reduction in road traffic injuries (n = 2). A few reviews of access to green space reported on improved social connectedness, reductions in perceived crime and improvements in mental health and well-being, with some reporting improved thermal comfort (through the cooling effect of vegetation) (Table 1). Environmental outcomes (GHG emissions) were generally not assessed, however some studies reported reduced vehicle kilometers traveled, thereby inferring a reduction in CO2 emissions—reflecting a lack of comprehensive assessments of benefits (for example, refs. 25,26).Reviews on neighborhood measures of urban greening (for example, tree planting, provision of green spaces) also reported reduced energy use, with mixed evidence of improved air quality and some evidence for increased biodiversity (Table 1). Recent studies relating to greening measures in low-income countries reported environmental benefits (for example, reduced soil erosion and flood risk47, improved water regulation and biodiversity45) and health benefits. For example, community gardens were associated with reduced outbreaks of infectious disease and air pollution60 and have contributed to improved food security61).Equity impactsOf the 22 reviews that considered impacts on equity, most (n = 16) found that there was inadequate information to assess equity in the component studies. Results from three housing reviews18,21,62 suggested reduced inequity by targeting low socioeconomic status or vulnerable groups, whereas three reviews suggested changes to the built environment to improve physical activity may benefit better-off groups more than others63,64,65.Summary of evidence and gapsMost evidence focused on climate mitigation actions in the transport and buildings sectors and on urban form, with limited evidence from the food and waste sectors. Health co-benefits were most frequently evidenced for actions that increased active transport or improved housing. Where reviews provided measures of effect, they suggested only modest impacts on climate mitigation, adaptation and health. Most evidence identified related to modest, single-sector interventions, with only 19 reviews describing actions in more than one sector (17 were in two sectors and two were in three sectors21,45)43,45,47,51,52,53,60,63,64,65,66,67,68,69,70,71,72. The cross-sectoral actions here mainly relate to transport and urban form, or buildings and urban form, rather than being the types of multisectoral action needed to address climate change11.Most reviews described actions but did not evaluate how they could be implemented (for example, through regulation (n = 5), subsidy and other incentives (n = 6)), with some exceptions for housing interventions (2/13 housing-specific evaluations), suggesting that researchers and city-level decision-makers have not yet focused on the regulatory and governance systems that are essential for scaling up action.Improvements to air quality were the main policy objective of implemented actions in several reviews (rather than a climate mitigation objective)40,43,51,73. Many city actions to reduce air pollution may also reduce GHG emissions (for example, from road transport74).We identified four critical policy implementation evidence gaps and potential structural barriers:(1) Lack of a transformative system approach to climate action. There is a dearth of complex, cross-sectoral, long-term, large-scale transformative actions required for deep decarbonization and sustainable and healthy cities. Driven by the sectoral division of city governments, a disconnect between public health, economic, transport, social and urban planning perspectives prevails, leading to fragmented policies and evaluations21,66(2) Failure to address externalities and trade-offs when assessing policy options. Traditional policy assessments rarely consider relevant costs and benefits systematically—for example, by focusing on travel time as the main metric of transport policy and ignoring public health benefits or carbon emission reductions39. Failing to anticipate trade-offs40 cultivates policy-driven market failures and emboldens opposition by interests adversely affected by the policy.(3) Lack of robustly designed impact evaluations during and after the implementation of policies. Most studies were focused on the implementation of a technological ‘solution’ (for example, greening of roofs)25,26,53, not the implementation of a policy to support uptake of ‘solutions’ including barriers and enablers and context-specific results. Many studies also had methodological weaknesses such as subjective outcome measures and insufficient follow-up periods63,66,69,71,75. Randomized and natural experimental evaluations (or quasi-experiments) were rare27.(4) Failure to engage community-driven initiatives. Participatory approaches, currently fragmented or unacknowledged, are critical for engaging communities in health and sustainability policy with the potential to reduce opposition to change and sustain progress through co-design and co-implementation of local actions61. This is particularly important in many low- and middle-income country contexts, where urban population growth is largely in informal settlements that are often neglected in the design of policies60 and is also relevant for wider climate justice including equitable adaptation76.DiscussionStrengths and limitationsA key strength of this umbrella review is that it synthesizes complex evidence from diverse sectors and settings on implemented actions at the city level to address climate change and health outcomes. Such evidence can be used to identify and advocate for those actions that deserve priority attention by city policy makers and local governments and also to identify evidence gaps.Limitations include the time it takes for primary research to be included in reviews, so our overview may not include the latest primary studies. Confidence in the findings of the primary studies was often not reported, and reviews did not generally perform adequate risk-of-bias assessments (Fig. 2).Gray literature and non-English-language sources were often excluded from existing reviews, and this could introduce substantial bias, if implemented and/or transformative actions are mainly reported in organizational evaluation and/or practice literature, rather than in peer-reviewed literature published in English.Comparison with other studies and reviewsTwo other recent umbrella reviews, despite different scale (national rather than urban)10 and objective (planning principles)21, came to similar conclusions about the paucity of robust evidence. Much of the existing evidence on actions to address climate change has come from modeling studies, particularly of actions in the transport sector74. A recent scoping review of modeling studies also identified that most climate and health evidence came from transport actions but additionally highlighted cross-sectoral mitigation and adaptation actions77.Our findings are also aligned to a recent narrative review on how cities can become carbon neutral and healthier through better urban and transport planning78. A recent overview79 recommends community engagement, government support and awareness raising for more effective policy action.An umbrella review of evidence on the health effects of greenhouse gas mitigation actions by the Lancet Pathfinder Commission10 using more restrictive methodological inclusion criteria than this analysis also found that included reviews presented modeled estimates with few examples of rigorously evaluated implemented actions and none at a transformational scale. In keeping with our findings, health impacts of implemented actions were mainly related to the promotion of active travel and public transport and, to a lesser extent, to reductions in air pollution. Increased consumption of healthy sustainable diets has great potential for climate mitigation and health benefits, but neither the Pathfinder review nor this review found evidence of relevant implemented actions.Implications for policyPositive framing in terms of health co-benefits helps to garner public and political10 support for climate action and can enable progress on both health and climate goals. We identified implications for policy regarding both the evaluation and implementation of sectoral actions (‘policy tools’ or ‘policy mechanisms’) that can be realized at pace and scale. We review the implications for sectoral policy from the umbrella review findings in the Supplementary Information (‘Implications for sectoral policies of the findings from the reviews’). Here we discuss more fundamental shifts towards ‘whole-of-city’ governance paradigms capable of overcoming structural barriers to integrated cross-sectoral action.Impacts of actions in cities to enhance environmental performance and improve health can occur at different scales—building, neighborhood or city. Concerted efforts are needed to transcend scales and sectors of the city, requiring action that can bring about transformational change11. Institutional fragmentation is commonly identified in research on urban governance80 and is thought to be a major barrier to urban transformation81. Transnational networks are working to improve coherence within and across cities (for example, Local Governments for Sustainability (ICLEI)82, C40 cities83, UN Programme on Human Settlements Programme84).We present four potential responses to the critical policy implementation evidence gaps and potential structural barriers identified above. Addressing these will involve various interest holders, including city-level decision-makers, research funders and national-level decision-makers.(1) Lack of a transformative system approach to climate action. Response: a new governance paradigm is needed to institutionalize transdisciplinary governance teams working across sectors and scales, embedding health and environment into core planning of city policies. Representation is required from public health; urban planning; transport and environmental and social sciences to co-design interventions21,22,66,67,69,75,85 with the engagement of affected communities (Challenge 4). Such a systems approach could break down policy silos85 and target the determinants of population health and sustainability64,70,86.(2) Failure to address externalities and trade-offs when assessing policy options. Response: systematic assessment of co-impacts before the implementation of a policy can enable more appropriate financing of sustainability and health policies in cities. Allocation of public financial resources and financial decision-making needs to capture the full societal return of implemented actions through expanded economic evaluation methods including valuation of a range of co-benefits from urban climate actions, reflecting long-term, intergenerational and health benefits39. For example, the inclusion of standardized health exposure or outcome metrics in the planning phase of urban policies (such as low-emission zones) often result in large benefit–cost ratios for urban climate actions19,39,73, particularly when combined with environmental parameters (for example, GHG emissions39, biodiversity impacts) or social equity benefits39,40. Assessment of trade-offs could identify, and address, potential sources of opposition by tailoring policies to local contexts and communicating the benefits of implementation effectively. The Pathfinder Initiative has suggested standardized approaches for reporting co-benefits intensity (years of life gained per 100,000 people) and climate mitigation intensity measures (kilotons of CO2e per 100,000 people) and for improving co-benefits modeling10,16.(3) Lack of robustly designed impact evaluations during and after the implementation of policies. Response: focusing resources on robust evaluation of policies and policy implementation can provide evidence and knowledge transfer to other settings (‘what works, how and when’). These evaluations can be conducted using a range of rigorous designs integrated, from inception27,40,75,85, using standardized, objective outcome measures26,40,63,66,87, alongside process evaluations to understand implementation, fidelity and causal mechanisms27,85, and economic evaluation of the full range of costs and benefits88. Where long-term monitoring is feasible, it can capture sustained effects and slow-paced changes63,85. Appropriate evaluations can provide contextually relevant evidence to guide policy, including whether to scale up, course correct, redesign or close down particular programs15. Research funders can build in evaluation funding alongside funding for implementation.(4) Failure to engage community-driven initiatives76. Response: adopt a governance structure that identifies, supports and scales up community-driven innovations rooted in existing social networks60,61 and integrates top-down policy with potential solutions identified at the grassroots, recognizing communities’ innovative capacity, and addressing socioeconomic causes of vulnerability to climate hazards and the distribution of adaptation resources89. Formal integration of co-design and co-implementation approaches into city planning and revised regulations may be required (for example, urban agriculture45, urban greening60,75, reusing waste and innovative housing45,60,75).We acknowledge that there are multiple political, economic and institutional challenges to the adoption and implementation of these potential policy responses. Future research and analysis should address these challenges as a priority.ConclusionsMany urban climate actions have substantial health co-benefits, particularly through increased physical activity, reduced air pollution, reducing exposure to extreme temperatures and increasing green space. However, such co-benefits were inconsistently quantified. Improved reporting on the interventions, comparisons, types of study and magnitudes of impacts in primary studies and systematic reviews is essential90.Our findings suggest that the greatest barrier to urban transformation is not a lack of knowledge of technical solutions (what to do) but rather a failure of the prevailing governance paradigms to deliver cross-sectoral policy actions (how to do it) at scale. We found no empirical documentation of transformative action at the city level. Except for some housing interventions, most implemented urban actions were those that are easily and relatively quickly set up (for example, travel plans, new bike lanes and so on), suggesting that there are structural barriers to action at the scale and pace needed. As the reported evidence was largely on single-sector interventions, our understanding of how interventions may interact, reinforce or conflict across domains is limited.Whereas national energy transitions are essential for achieving Paris Agreement targets3, implementation and evaluation of transformative urban climate and health actions are crucial for addressing climate and public health challenges. This includes developing and testing new models of governance to overcome deep-seated barriers to the effective design and implementation of policies, programs and interventions. These should support multisectoral systems approaches, the upscaling of effective community-driven innovations and improved financing of healthy and sustainable cities supported by robust outcome monitoring and the incorporation of well-designed evaluations into policy and planning from the inception phase.MethodsPathways to environment and health from city-level actions to address climate changeWe developed a conceptual framework building on the DPSEEA (Drivers, Pressures, State, Exposure, Effect, Action)91,92 and other relevant frameworks3,21,93 to describe how city climate actions relate to environment and population-level health impacts (Fig. 3). We applied this framework to map the impacts of mitigation and adaptation actions from relevant sectors in an umbrella review of the published literature. Transport, buildings, waste, food and urban form were selected as relevant sectors with policy objectives and types of action identified by the UK Climate Change Committee94, Project Drawdown95, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change4 and the C40 Cities Climate Leadership Group96 and other urban initiatives97,98 (policy objectives are summarized below and further detail and associated types of action are given in Supplementary Table 2). We define ‘urban form’ interventions as any design or planning actions that enhance liveability and/or environmental performance, including several actions relating to transport (provision of walking and cycling paths, traffic calming infrastructure) and buildings (green buildings). We define city-level action as city wide, or at least at neighborhood level.We identified the following sector specific policy objectives for decreasing GHG emissions (Supplementary Table 2):
                
                  Transport—decrease VKT through reduced journeys, mode shift and active travel; and decrease CO2e GHG emissions per VKT through improved vehicle efficiency and electric vehicles
                
              
                
                  Buildings (both through construction and operation)—lower energy use; increase energy efficiency; promote low-GHG emission energy sources; foster low embodied GHG emission construction
                
              
                
                  Waste (both through solid waste and wastewater)—transition to a circular economy; energy recovery (for example, from incineration)
                
              
                
                  Food—encourage low-GHG-emission diets (for example, increase consumption of plant-based foods); reduce dietary footprints (for example, reduce food miles); reduce food loss and waste
                
              For urban form—policy objectives for climate mitigation and adaptation relate to the physical characteristics of cities through improving liveability (for example, through neighborhood design) and enhancing environmental performance (for example, expanding green space).We identified the following pathways linking mitigation and/or adaptation actions to health in cities (Table 2) and used these to identify relevant actions. Actions in urban settings where the primary aim is to:
                
                  (1)
                  
                    reduce GHG emissions with accompanying co-impacts on health (for example, adoption of clean renewable energy sources, retrofitting houses for energy efficiency, promotion of zero-emission vehicles or plant-forward diets);
                  
                
                
                  (2)
                  
                    reduce the use of finite natural resources or use natural resources more sustainably and as an ancillary consequence also reduce GHG emissions with accompanying co-impacts on health (for example, reuse of water resources and recycling);
                  
                
                
                  (3)
                  
                    reduce the health effects from the impacts of climate change (climate adaptation strategies, for example, heatwave and vector-borne disease early-warning systems, flood defences, shading and green infrastructure);
                  
                
                
                  (4)
                  
                    improve public health with GHG emission co-impacts (for example, improved infrastructure for water and sanitation, increased cycle lanes to promote active travel).
                  
                
              Some actions (for example, nature-based solutions) may be classified under more than one action type depending on the primary aims and outcomes, including so-called ‘triple-win’ solutions such as shifts to green, blue and hybrid infrastructure, which provide immediate health benefits and support both adaptation and carbon storage (mitigation)99,100.Umbrella reviewAn umbrella review is useful in identifying the weight of systematic evidence in disparate areas. It builds on the strengths of depth of analysis in individual reviews, which often focus on narrowly defined topic areas, adding breadth of analysis by summarizing the evidence from reviews in multiple dimensions, often cutting across academic fields to produce cross-disciplinary policy-relevant findings5,17. This review was intended to provide an evidence base on the effectiveness of implemented climate change mitigation and adaptation actions at city level and their impacts on health and environmental outcomes. The review was carried out following a protocol registered with PROSPERO (CRD42024607168)101, and deviations from the protocol are reported below.Inclusion and exclusion criteriaThe inclusion criteria were defined a priori by the research team using the conceptual framework and the pathways identified, as reflected in the PICOS statement adapted for umbrella reviews (Table 3).Evidence from any global region or income status was eligible, including low-, middle- and/or high-income countries.The focus of the review is on urban sustainability and health, specifically city-level interventions with potential health co-benefits, implemented to address climate change in five sectors: transport, buildings, waste, food and/or urban form (for example, liveability). We included studies of interventions (termed ‘actions’), which are implemented policies, programs, projects and other types of action by public and private bodies (for example, subsidized public transport), which might include promotion of specific technologies (for example, an e-scooter). The intervention refers to the policy, program or action that was implemented (for example, subsidized public transport), as opposed to the technology being used (for example, an e-scooter). In contrast, reviews solely concerning technological solutions, rather than implemented actions, were excluded. We developed a taxonomy of policy objectives in various sectors that reflects many of the principal targets for policy action by cities on climate change mitigation and adaptation. The actions included policies, programs, interventions and actions that affect urban climate goals for health outcomes and/or environmental outcomes that are plausibly on the pathways to health impacts.We excluded interventions with no obvious relevance to climate mitigation or adaptation, such as those associated with exposure to tobacco smoking and lead exposure. An example of a review of interventions with no ambition to address climate change was Rana et al.102, which reviewed the impact of COVID-19 pandemic lockdowns on air quality and was therefore excluded. We excluded studies that did not evaluate implemented interventions and actions; for example, Spence et al.103 reviewed predicted movement behavior and transport mode choice for autonomous vehicle uptake scenarios. We also excluded studies that focused solely on determinants of actions; for example, Oluleye et al.104 reviewed barriers to and enablers of circular economy adoption.The comparison concerns the counterfactual condition, which could be measured contemporaneously (that is, a controlled study) or historically (for example, before versus after study or interrupted time series). Eligible reviews included active comparisons, which compared different types of intervention for achieving the policy objective, passive comparisons, which compared a new intervention with business as usual (BAU) or standard practice in the sector and pipeline comparisons that made comparisons with a population or area which was set to receive the intervention at a future date. The comparison condition was usually implicitly BAU but was often not articulated clearly in the reviews. The likely effect of an intervention might be greater or lesser, depending on the nature of the counterfactual, and is therefore crucially important for determining the relevance (external validity) and transferability of the findings.Outcomes were measured or modeled environmental and health outcomes. Environmental outcomes included any climate active pollutants such as CO2 and other GHGs and air pollution. Health outcomes included morbidity or mortality, physical activity and nutrition. We also included exposures that were close proxies for environment and health outcomes, principally to incorporate co-benefits of climate change adaptation measures including heat, thermal comfort, shade cover, disaster risk exposure, diet and changes to modal transport share. Information on inequalities, adverse consequences and non-health co-benefits (such as social cohesion) were eligible as secondary outcomes. We excluded studies that measured intermediate outcomes only, such as attitudes or behaviors. Such excluded studies included those which: examined motives and barriers to physical activity in different built environments105; focused on actions to facilitate adoption of low-emission vehicles without reporting a health or climate outcome or a proxy outcome106; reviewed heat vulnerability indexes107 and several reviews of plastic waste108, e-waste109 and household and community recycling110, none of which measured greenhouse gas emissions or health risks (for example110, reported a meta-analysis of psychosocial interventions on recycling behavior). In addition, one review111 was excluded because it reported interventions relating only to childhood obesity which were not climate relevant.Regarding eligible types of study, we included systematic reviews of interventions (implemented actions) that presented critically appraised evidence from existing literature, defined as studies that contain: (1) a well-defined question for the review; (2) an explicit strategy to search literature over a defined time period; (3) transparent criteria for the inclusion or exclusion of studies; (4) systematic coding and critical appraisal of included studies and (5) a systematic synthesis of study findings112. In addition, although particular aspects of the review, such as inclusion decisions and data coding, should be conducted, independently, by more than one team member13, we did not exclude reviews which undertook coding by a single reviewer. Where review studies met the criteria, but only a portion of the component studies were focused on our target sectors (for example, ref. 71), we focused on the authors’ conclusions for the component studies that met our criteria. We excluded other types of systematic evidence, such as systematic maps (for example, refs. 113,114) or scoping reviews (for example, ref. 115) that did not synthesize the findings from the included evidence. We also excluded the following study types: theoretical reviews (for example, ref. 115), methodology studies (for example, ref. 116), reviews of health or environmental impact of current environmental quality (unless component studies were comparison studies or natural experiments), plans or guidelines117,118, unless the latter included a systematic review of actions on which the guidelines were based. We also excluded occupational studies.Search strategyWe searched for systematic reviews published in English from January 2009 to May 2024. Key search terms were determined using published strategies covering environmental terms and study types and tested using a systematic approach119,120 and refined by the authors to reflect the scope of the project. The search strategy was based on three blocks—terms relating to implemented actions (for example, green space, watershed management, waste, traffic), climate change and the environment (for example, flood, heatwave, erosion, pollution) and cities (for example, neighborhood, built environment)—and an example search strategy is given in the Supplementary Information (‘Example search strategy results—Ovid Global Health’). Thirteen databases were selected to retrieve research literature from the fields of health, environmental sciences and the built environment. They included: OvidSP Medline ALL, OvidSP Embase Classic+Embase; OvidSP Global Health; OvidSP Econlit; OvidSP Food Science & Technology Abstracts; OvidSP CAB Abstracts; OvidSP Geobase; EBSCOhost Africa-Wide Information; EBSCOhost GreenFILE; Web of Science Core Collection, consisting of Science Citation Index Expanded, Social Sciences Citation Index, Arts & Humanities Citation Index, Emerging Sources Citation Index; Web of Science BIOSIS; Scopus; and TRID. Full search strategies for all databases are available in ref. 120.To ensure a comprehensive retrieval of relevant literature, the database searches were executed independently on three separate occasions. This iterative process was designed to capture any updates or additions to the databases between different search periods. Consequently, the search protocol resulted in the retrieval of duplicate records not only between different databases but also across the three distinct search iterations. These duplicates were systematically identified and removed during the subsequent screening process.Data extraction and synthesisScreening of titles and abstract was completed by pairs of reviewers working independently. Disagreements were discussed to reach consensus, or by involving a third author as arbiter. The selected papers were categorized according to the sector where action would be taken (transport, buildings, waste, food and/or urban form) and in some cases papers contributed to findings in multiple sectors. Full-text data extraction was divided by sector and extracted using a standardized process to capture information about author, year, study design, aim, context, intervention(s), outcome (type) and findings. Reviews were appraised using AMSTAR2121, which was developed to evaluate systematic reviews on health topics. We adjusted the critical scoring items removing those aspects we thought would not lead to serious bias in the review findings, in a field where the application of systematic review methodology and standards of reporting are more nascent than in health. For example, authors may be constrained by journal word counts in reporting lists of studies excluded at full-text stage; risk-of-bias assessment tools need further development to adequately appraise quasi-experiments and natural experimental evaluations122. We therefore included the following critical items to generate the confidence assessments: articulation of the inclusion criteria for the review (population, intervention, comparator, outcome and study design), comprehensive search strategy, duplicate study selection and data extraction, description of studies, meta-analysis methods, analysis of heterogeneity and conflicts of interest. Reviews assessed as providing critically low-confidence evidence were excluded from the summary of findings.Results were summarized narratively, according to the sectors and outcomes defined above, from reviews that were assessed as at high, medium or low confidence. We aimed to report evidence identified on implemented interventions in relation to each policy goal in each sector and, where possible, an estimate of the magnitude of the impact on health and climate active pollutants (CAP) or other environmental outcome. We aimed to extract review-level (pooled effect) estimates of the magnitudes of impacts on health and emissions or other environmental outcomes, using comparable metrics, alongside 95% confidence intervals (Table 1). Where the reviews did not provide information about magnitudes of effect, we extracted qualitative information about the direction of effect and possible moderators.Deviations from protocolWe made three main deviations from the study protocol. The first was to modify the AMSTAR2 systematic review critical appraisal tool121, to consolidate sections on randomized controlled trials and non-randomized studies of interventions (that is, quasi-experiments and natural experimental evaluations). This was done because nearly all primary studies contained in the reviews used quasi-experimental study designs. Secondly, whereas we aimed to extract effect size quantities (point estimates and 95% confidence intervals) associated with particular interventions, we were only able to do so for a minority of reviews. Doing so consistently requires extracting data from the primary studies on which the reviews were based, an approach taken in other reviews of reviews (for example, ref. 10) but beyond the scope of this research. Thirdly, an important finding of our umbrella review was that a lack of integrated, multisectoral policies was a barrier to the transformational change required to achieve climate and health goals across several reviews. Therefore, we created a summary of challenges and implications for improved governance drawing on information from the included reviews.Reporting summaryFurther information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

items.body:
Giulio Regeni, dopo 7 anni gli agenti egiziani vanno a processo

In Lombardia l’inquinamento da PM2.5 costa 33,4 miliardi di euro all’anno
		
		
			Il PM2.5 costa alla Lombardia 33,4 miliardi di euro l’anno, il 7,3 per cento del Pil regionale. Cittadini per l’Aria presenta un esposto alla Corte dei Conti.

Italia
			22 settembre 2026
			
				di Luigi Mastrodonato

Educazione affettiva nelle scuole, raggiunte le 500mila firme per il referendum
		
		
			L’obiettivo è abrogare i limiti introdotti dalle legge Valditara, che prevedono divieti fino alle scuole medie e consenso informato scritto dei genitori. 
		
		
			 Diritti
			9 settembre 2026
			
				di Simone Santi

Il Veneto approva il fine vita: è la quarta Regione a farlo
		
		
			Via libera alla proposta Liberi Subito dell’Associazione Luca Coscioni, che riprende la sentenza della Consulta in mancanza di una legge nazionale. 
		
		
			 Diritti
			3 settembre 2026
			
				di Simone Santi

Liberi di scegliere: il progetto per salvare i giovani nati in contesti mafiosi
			
			
				Il programma di recupero di minorenni e giovani adulti cresciuti in famiglie legate alla criminalità, nato a Reggio Calabria, sta per diventare nazionale.

Italia

15 luglio 2026

Il ddl sulla caccia ha il primo via libera tra le proteste delle associazioni
			
			
				Via libera del Senato al disegno di legge che allarga le aree venatorie, allunga i calendari, depotenzia l’Ispra e aumenta le specie cacciabili.

Ambiente

24 giugno 2026

Curarsi in Italia ormai è un diritto che dipende dalle zone e dal reddito
			
			
				5,8 milioni di italiani rinunciano a curarsi. Il report di Medici del mondo evidenza disuguaglianze sociali e territoriali.

Diritti

16 giugno 2026

Sovraffollamento, suicidi, diritti negati: il sistema delle carceri è “tutto chiuso”
			
			
				Il rapporto di Antigone mostra il volto più scuro dei nostri istituti penitenziari: luoghi da cui è sempre più difficile uscire pronti al reinserimento.

Italia

19 maggio 2026

Arriva il salario giusto: cos’è e cosa cambia rispetto al salario minimo
			
			
				Nessuna cifra oraria a priori, ma l’obbligo a conformarsi al contratto collettivo nazionale più rappresentativo: la risposta del governo ai 9 euro l’ora.

Diritti

12 maggio 2026

Referendum sulla giustizia, ha vinto il No
			
			
				L’affluenza ha sfiorato il 60 per cento, e la maggioranza degli italiani boccia la riforma: il No è intorno al 53,7 percento.

Italia

23 marzo 2026

items.body:
ottobre
		
			Rom-E 2026: il futuro della mobilità al centro del dibattito
		
		
			Rom-E 2026 apre la sua sesta edizione con un confronto sul futuro dell’automotive, tra transizione, mercato, nuove regole e bisogni emergenti.
		
					
									Roma
											 Evento diffuso

Noleggio sociale: cos’è, i requisiti per beneficiarne e come richiederlo
			
			
				Con 100 euro al mese si potrà noleggiare un’auto a basse emissioni. Il noleggio sociale è rivolto a chi ha Isee inferiore a 30mila euro e un’auto inquinante da rottamare.

Auto

12 agosto 2026

L’avanzata elettrica della Cina non si arresta
			
			
				Da mesi in vetta alla classifica delle auto elettriche più vendute, Leapmotor presenta la nuova B05. Compatta e accessibile, l’abbiamo provata.

Auto

9 agosto 2026

Non solo elettrico: cosa sappiamo del nuovo brand cinese che punta sull’accessibilità
			
			
				Accessibile, design ispirato alla natura, ibrido o (preferibilmente) elettrico: come va e cosa offre il nuovo suv compatto di GWM.

Auto

2 agosto 2026

Ogliastra, viaggio nel dietro le quinte di un docufilm che racconta la formula segreta della longevità.
			
			
				Giuseppe Bertuccio D’Angelo. Gli incontri sorprendenti, le strade di montagna e i silenzi assordanti. Vi porto con me nell’isola dei centenari alla scoperta delle Blue zone dell’Ogliastra.

Mobilità e turismo

21 luglio 2026

Montagna d’estate, in Alto Adige istituiti i ranger per sensibilizzare e informare i turisti
			
			
				Dal lago di Carezza al Seceda, i luoghi simbolo dell’Alto Adige saranno presidiati da 15 ranger che si occuperanno di controllo, sensibilizzazione, informazione.

Mobilità e turismo

18 luglio 2026

Hyundai e la Water Defenders Alliance approdano a Livorno per proteggere un mare ricco di biodiversità
			
			
				Dopo Milano, il progetto realizzato con LifeGate nell’ambito della Water Defenders Alliance arriva nel porto toscano. Obiettivo: prevenire l’inquinamento delle acque attraverso una tecnologia in grado di assorbire oli e idrocarburi.

Ambiente

8 luglio 2026
